Price Production and Consumption Separately

A Two-Track Architecture for Carbon Pricing in Open Economies

Author

Stephen J. Stretton

Published

October 2026

Abstract

A carbon tax on domestic production does two jobs at once: it rewards firms for cutting emissions per unit of output, and it charges for the carbon in what the economy consumes. In an open economy the second job undermines the first, because the charge falls on exports and spares imports. This paper separates the jobs. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production intensity; a destination-based charge, levied through the value-added tax and through forward-announced obligations on energy suppliers, prices consumption. I show that the two tracks together reproduce the Pigouvian allocation for domestic consumption without leakage, that the feebate’s residual cost is second order, that international payments above half the feebate rate make adoption a net gain, and that destination charges make each exporter’s most competitive feebate rate equal to the charge in its markets. A calibration to the EU’s default emission values for steel illustrates the magnitudes.

Keywords

carbon pricing, feebates, output-based rebating, border carbon adjustment, destination-based taxation, policy crediting, carbon leakage

In brief

Carbon prices stay low in open economies because one instrument does two jobs: it pushes producers to cut emissions per unit of output, and it makes consumers pay for the carbon they use. This brief separates the jobs. A revenue-neutral feebate prices production intensity at no cost to the treasury and with a small price effect. A carbon component of VAT and forward-announced obligations on energy suppliers price consumption, imports included. A carbon-price-equivalent metric measures both. International payments above half the feebate rate make adoption a net gain, and destination-based charges turn leakage into a race to the top.

Working paper, version 0.3, October 2026. Stephen J. Stretton, writing in a personal capacity. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 1.1.

1 Introduction

Explicit carbon prices cover about 28 percent of global emissions, at an emissions-weighted average of about $5 per tonne, far below the range the High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices judged consistent with the Paris temperature goals, $50–100 per tonne by 2030 (World Bank 2025; High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices 2017). The usual explanation is political will. This paper argues that the gap is also built into the instrument.

A conventional carbon price, a tax or an emissions trading system covering domestic emitters, is levied on the origin basis: it falls on what a country produces. It therefore does two jobs with one rate. It gives each firm an incentive to cut emissions per unit of output, the intensity margin. And it raises the price of carbon-intensive goods, so that buyers use less of them, the quantity margin. In a closed economy both jobs are welcome and one rate does both efficiently. In an open economy the second job is done badly. The price rise falls on exports, which compete against unpriced foreign supply, and spares imports, which displace domestic production. Part of the quantity response is leakage rather than abatement, and the competitive loss is concentrated in the energy-intensive, trade-exposed sectors that hold most industrial emissions. Governments respond by exempting those sectors, allocating permits free or keeping the rate low (Keen et al. 2022). A border adjustment on imports, such as the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (European Parliament and Council 2023), protects the home market but leaves exports exposed and recognizes only explicit carbon prices paid abroad.

This paper proposes giving each job its own instrument. The production track prices intensity with a revenue-neutral feebate: each producer pays \(t(e_i - \bar e)\) per unit of output, a charge above a sector benchmark \(\bar e\) and a rebate below it. “Production” here means production in the economic and trade sense, what a country makes for home use or for export, and the metric is emissions per unit of physical output, or per dollar of output where products differ. The consumption track prices what is consumed at home, whatever its origin, with a destination-based charge on embodied carbon. It has two parts: a carbon component of the value-added tax (VAT) on goods, with imports charged and exports zero-rated, and a forward-announced legal obligation on the few large firms that supply energy for domestic use: fuel for heating and transport. Electricity sold to final users bears the consumption-track price on its generation carbon, net of any carbon price paid upstream: through the VAT carbon component where one exists, through the supplier obligation where it does not. A measurement framework, a carbon-price-equivalent metric of the kind Black et al. (2022) compute with a full model, puts every instrument, price-based or not, on one scale. Electricity generation is on the production track, priced on the same intensity metric; the separate case for doing so turns on capital turnover and household prices rather than trade, and is made in the companion paper on feebates (Stretton 2026c).

The paper makes four contributions.

  1. An equivalence result (Section 4). With a common rate, the two tracks reproduce the Pigouvian allocation for domestic consumption and production intensity, with no leakage through the goods channel. This is a clean, implementable statement of a known allocation result (Stephen P. Holland 2012; Markusen 1975); what is new is its corollary on revenue, which tells finance ministries which countries gain and which lose: the difference from a Pigouvian origin tax equals the charge on carbon in net exports.
  2. The cost of the production track (Section 5). A revenue-neutral feebate costs the treasury nothing and raises the producer price only by the resource cost of abatement, \(\tfrac12 t\,\Delta e\), roughly a third of the price effect of a tax in the calibrated steel example (Section 6). Its weakness, the absence of an output signal, has a precise size, and the consumption track removes it.
  3. A self-interested case for policy crediting (Section 7). If an outside buyer pays \(\pi\) per tonne abated and the host keeps the reduction toward its own target, a feebate is a net gain to the adopting country whenever \(\pi > t/2\), the threshold Strand (2020) derives for a donor-supported carbon tax, and the country’s best response is \(t = \pi\).
  4. From leakage to a race to the top (Section 8). Once importers charge for embodied carbon, each exporter’s most competitive feebate rate equals the charge in its markets. In a calibrated simulation the average embodied intensity of steel imports falls by more than half when exporters respond.

The paper anchors a series. The consumption track is developed in Stretton (2026a), the feebate design in Stretton (2026c), the measurement framework in Stretton (2026d), and the reform of the EU’s border mechanism in Stretton (2026b).

2 Related literature

The paper connects five literatures. Appendix A reviews them in detail.

Leakage and competitiveness. Unilateral carbon pricing shifts emissions-intensive production abroad. Model-based estimates of leakage rates for energy-intensive, trade-exposed sectors range from 5 to 25 percent, with a mean of 14 (Branger and Quirion 2014). Ex-post studies find little or no leakage at the EU’s past carbon prices, partly because free allocation shielded industry (Naegele and Zaklan 2019; Dechezleprêtre et al. 2022; Colmer et al. 2025), so the problem is prospective: it bites at the $80–100 rates this paper is about. Pass-through of carbon costs ranges from under half in EU trade-exposed sectors (Neuhoff and Ritz 2019) to about 70 percent in US domestic-market manufacturing (Ganapati et al. 2020), a difference that itself reflects trade exposure. The theoretical case for border adjustment when carbon prices differ across countries is established: Markusen (1975) shows that with international externalities optimal policy combines production and consumption taxes, and Keen and Kotsogiannis (2014) show that border tax adjustments are needed for Pareto efficiency when carbon prices are not equalized.

Border carbon adjustment. The design literature (Ismer and Neuhoff 2007; Mehling et al. 2019; Cosbey et al. 2019; Keen et al. 2022) establishes the main choices: sectoral coverage, measurement of embodied carbon (domestic benchmark, country default or firm-specific data), treatment of exports and recognition of foreign policy. Keen, Parry and Roaf note the tension this paper builds on: a border adjustment in the VAT sense puts tax on a destination basis, while the Paris Agreement assigns responsibility on an origin basis.

Output-based rebating and intensity standards. Output-based allocation, tradable performance standards and feebates price intensity but subsidize output relative to a tax (Carolyn Fischer 2001; C. Fischer and Fox 2007; Carolyn Fischer and Fox 2012). Stephen P. Holland et al. (2009) show that an intensity standard can even raise emissions when the implicit output subsidy is large, and Fowlie et al. (2016) show, for cement, that output-based allocation can outperform auctioning once leakage and market power are counted. Keen et al. (2022) classify feebates and output-based rebates as cutting intensity but not output. This paper takes that weakness as given and assigns the output margin to a separate instrument.

Destination-based taxation. VAT spread across most of the world within half a century (Keen and Lockwood 2010). For a uniform tax, the destination and origin bases are trade-neutral (Lockwood and Whalley 2010); the trade effects in this paper come from charges that vary with carbon intensity, not from the destination basis as such. The same logic underlies proposals for destination-based corporate taxation (Devereux et al. 2021). Consumption-based emissions accounting shows that high-income countries’ consumption footprints exceed their territorial emissions (Peters and Hertwich 2008; Grubb et al. 2022).

International incentives. Climate clubs use border measures to induce participation (Nordhaus 2015); Helm et al. (2012) analyze the strategic use of border adjustments; Parry et al. (2021) propose an international carbon price floor among large emitters, with non-price measures counted through their carbon-price equivalents (Black et al. 2022). Results-based climate finance pays for verified reductions. Project crediting has a poor record on additionality: Probst et al. (2024) find that under 16 percent of credits represent real reductions, and Calel et al. (2025) that at least 52 percent of Indian wind credits under the Clean Development Mechanism were non-additional. Strand (2020) derives the payment that makes a donor-supported carbon tax worthwhile for the host.

What is new. The split is old in theory. Markusen (1975) showed that with an international externality optimal policy taxes both production and consumption; Weisbach et al. (2023) restate this with an extraction leg; and Stephen P. Holland (2012) proves that an intensity standard combined with a consumption tax can reach the first best under leakage. It also has close policy precedents: Grubb et al. (2022) list the separation of production incentives from a charge on the use of carbon-intensive materials as a trade-compatible option, Pollitt et al. (2020) estimate that a consumption charge on basic materials at about €80/tCO₂ adds roughly 10 percent to emission cuts without leakage, and Neuhoff et al. (2026) propose benchmark-based free allocation with a standardized liability per tonne of material. Against that work this paper claims five things: (i) a specific pairing of a revenue-neutral, updated-benchmark feebate, which needs no emissions trading system and can be adopted by a developing country alone, with a carbon component of VAT across all goods and forward-announced energy obligations; (ii) the closed-form residual cost of the feebate and its calibration to the EU’s default intensities for steel; (iii) the exporter best-response result under intensity-based destination charges; (iv) the extension of Strand’s crediting threshold to feebates, with the best response \(t = \pi\); and (v) the use of a carbon-price equivalent to make non-price production instruments creditable and recognizable at the border.

3 Model

Technology. A competitive sector produces a homogeneous good. A producer choosing emissions intensity \(e\) (tonnes of CO₂ per unit of output) has unit cost \[ c(e) = c_0 + \frac{k}{2}\,(e_0 - e)^2, \qquad e \le e_0, \tag{1}\] where \(e_0\) is the intensity chosen with no carbon policy and \(k > 0\) is the slope of the marginal cost of reducing intensity. The marginal abatement cost per unit of intensity is \(k(e_0 - e)\). With competitive pricing and no policy, the price is \(p_0 = c_0\).

Demand. Home consumption \(D(p)\) and foreign demand for home exports \(X(p)\) have price elasticities \(\eta_D\) and \(\eta_X\). In Section 8, an importing market buys from several exporters under Armington demand (Armington 1969), with elasticity of substitution \(\sigma\) among sources.

Instruments. Three instruments, each at a rate per tonne of CO₂:

  • an origin tax \(t\): a producer pays \(t\,e\) per unit produced, whether sold at home or exported;
  • a feebate \(t\): a producer pays \(t\,(e - \bar e)\) per unit produced, with \(\bar e\) the sector’s output-weighted average intensity, so that payments sum to zero;
  • a destination charge \(\tau\): each unit consumed at home pays \(\tau\,m\), where \(m\) is its embodied intensity, whether produced at home or imported; exports are zero-rated.

The feebate benchmark is updated to the realized average, so an individual firm’s choice moves \(\bar e\) only through its own output share. With many firms that effect is negligible, and the firm treats \(\bar e\) as given.

4 The equivalence result

Proposition 1 (equivalence). Let the home country apply a feebate at rate \(t\) and a destination charge at rate \(\tau = t\), and let embodied intensity be measured accurately. Then (i) home producers choose the same intensity as under a Pigouvian origin tax at rate \(t\); (ii) home consumers face the same price as under that tax for home-produced goods, and the full carbon cost of imported goods; (iii) home exports bear no domestic carbon charge beyond the resource cost of abatement. Revenue is \(t\) times the carbon embodied in home consumption, compared with \(t\) times the carbon in home production under the origin tax; the difference is \(t\) times the carbon in net exports.

The proof is in Appendix B. The intuition is that a Pigouvian price does two things a feebate and a destination charge can each do separately. The marginal cost of emitting, \(t\), is the same under a feebate and a tax, so producers choose the same intensity. The average cost of emitting, \(t\,e\), is moved from the producer to the consumer: the feebate removes it from the producer price, and the destination charge adds it back to the consumer price for everything consumed at home. Because the charge applies to imports at their own embodied intensity, foreign producers cannot undercut home producers by being dirtier, and there is no leakage on the consumption base.

Figure 1 shows the incidence in a stylized steel market. Under an origin tax, home producers carry the carbon charge whether they sell at home or abroad, and imports carry none. A border adjustment on imports fixes the home market but not exports. The two tracks charge home sales and imports alike, and leave exports with only the resource cost of abatement.

Three qualifications matter. First, equivalence holds for the home country’s consumption; it says nothing about emissions embodied in home exports, which are priced, on the consumption track, by the importer. That is the subject of Section 8. Second, the result requires the destination charge to be measured on actual embodied intensity, at least for large importers that choose to verify; default values deliberately set high, as in the EU’s regime (European Commission 2025), preserve the incentive to verify but tax average importers above their true intensity. Third, the feebate and the destination charge need not share a rate. The production rate \(t\) can be set higher than the consumption rate \(\tau\), because it does not raise average costs; the consumption rate is set by what households will accept and by the revenue the VAT reform needs (Section 9). Fourth, the result removes leakage through the goods channel only. A coalition that cuts fossil-fuel demand lowers world fuel prices and raises use elsewhere; no border measure on goods addresses that channel, which in model studies is as large as the goods channel or larger (Branger and Quirion 2014; Weisbach et al. 2023). The production track in exporting countries, which is the subject of Section 8, is the response to it (Jakob et al. 2014).

Corollary (revenue). Revenue from the two tracks is \(\tau\,M_C\), where \(M_C\) is carbon embodied in home consumption, against \(t\,E_P\) under an origin tax, where \(E_P\) is carbon emitted in home production. A net exporter of embodied carbon raises less; a net importer raises more. This is the fiscal counterpart of the distinction between production-based and consumption-based emissions accounts (Peters and Hertwich 2008).

5 What the production track costs

Proposition 2 (intensity). A feebate and an origin tax at the same rate induce the same intensity, \(e^* = e_0 - t/k\).

Proposition 3 (residual cost). Under a revenue-neutral feebate the producer price rises by \[ \Delta p_F = c(e^*) - c_0 = \frac{t^2}{2k} = \tfrac12\, t\, \Delta e , \tag{2}\] the resource cost of abatement, while under an origin tax it rises by \(t e_0 - t^2/2k\). The ratio is \(\Delta e/(2e_0 - \Delta e)\). Output falls by \(\eta\, t^2 / (2 k p_0)\) in proportion under the feebate, second order in \(t\), and by about \(\eta\, t e_0 / p_0\) under the tax, first order.

The feebate’s treasury cost is zero by construction. Its economic cost to producers is the cost of the abatement itself, which a tax also imposes; what it removes is the tax on the remaining emissions, the infra-marginal carbon bill. For a 30 percent cut in intensity, the feebate raises the price by 18 percent as much as a tax at the same rate; for a 48 percent cut, by about a third.

Proposition 4 (the output margin). To cut the same tonnes as an origin tax at rate \(t_T\), a feebate alone needs the rate \[ t_F = t_T\left(1 + \frac{\eta\, k\, e_0^2}{p_0}\right) \tag{3}\] to first order. The premium rises with the price elasticity of demand, with carbon intensity per dollar of output and with the steepness of abatement costs.

This is the known weakness of intensity-based instruments (Stephen P. Holland et al. 2009; Carolyn Fischer and Fox 2012). In economy-wide simulations, feebate packages achieve roughly 50–70 percent of the emission cuts of a carbon tax at the same rate (International Monetary Fund 2019). Two features of the open-economy setting limit it. In a trade-exposed sector, much of a tax’s output response is foreign supply replacing home supply: it reduces home emissions but not global emissions. The premium in equation 3 is therefore an upper bound on the feebate’s disadvantage from a global view, reached only when \(\eta\) reflects genuine demand reduction. And the consumption track restores genuine demand reduction on the consumption base. The architecture, not the feebate alone, delivers both margins.

Heterogeneous firms. Let firms differ in baseline intensity \(e_{0i}\) and abatement slope \(k_i\), with output shares \(s_i\). Under a feebate the benchmark is \(\bar e = \sum_i s_i e_i^*\) and firm \(i\)’s unit cost becomes \(c_i(e_i^*) + t(e_i^* - \bar e)\). Two consequences follow.

  1. Reallocation. Costs rise for firms dirtier than the benchmark and fall for cleaner ones, so output moves toward clean producers within the sector. This within-sector reallocation is part of the feebate’s abatement, and it does not depend on a fall in total sector output.
  2. Price effects depend on the price-setting firm. With a competitive fringe, the market price follows the marginal producer’s cost. If the marginal producer is dirtier than the benchmark, the price rises by more than equation 2; if cleaner, it can fall, and total output can rise.

Proposition 5 (sign condition). Under a revenue-neutral feebate, sector output falls relative to no policy if and only if the price-setting producer’s net feebate payment plus its abatement cost is positive: \(t(e_m^* - \bar e) + \tfrac12 t\,\Delta e_m > 0\), where \(m\) indexes the marginal producer. With identical firms the condition always holds, so total emissions fall. With a clean marginal producer and a benchmark well above its intensity it can fail, which is the case Stephen P. Holland et al. (2009) warn against. Updating the benchmark to the realized average and excluding new entrants’ output from the benchmark calculation for an initial period are the design responses (Stretton 2026c).

Windfalls. Firms that are already clean receive rebates from the first year. Relative to a tax, the feebate transfers the infra-marginal carbon bill from dirty firms to clean ones rather than to the treasury. Relative to free allocation by historical output, as in most emissions trading systems, the transfer is targeted at performance rather than at incumbency.

6 A calibrated illustration: steel

The illustration uses the EU’s default values for embodied emissions in hot-rolled flat steel (CN 7208), adopted under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621 (European Commission 2025). Direct emissions intensities range from 2.1 tCO₂ per tonne (Japan, South Korea) through 2.4 (Türkiye) and 3.2 (China) to 4.3 (India) and 8.2 (Indonesia), reflecting differences in production route (blast furnace versus electric arc furnace) and in the coal intensity of iron-making. The rest of the calibration is stylized and labelled so: a base price of $600 per tonne for every exporter, and an abatement slope \(k_i\) set so that a rate of $50/tCO₂ cuts each exporter’s intensity by 30 percent. At $80/tCO₂ the cut is 48 percent.

Table 1 and Figure 2 compare the price effect of a tax and a feebate at $80/tCO₂. The tax raises the producer price by 21–43 percent for exporters other than Indonesia; the feebate by 7–14 percent. The ratio is constant across exporters, at about 0.32, because the proportional intensity cut is the same; it is the infra-marginal carbon bill that the feebate removes.

Two lessons follow for developing-country exporters. A production feebate at a rate comparable to the EU’s carbon price is affordable: it raises costs by a single-digit percentage for most exporters, against a quarter to two-fifths for a tax. And the most carbon-intensive producers have the most to gain from adopting one, because their tax liability, which the feebate avoids, is largest.

7 International payments and policy crediting

Suppose an outside buyer pays \(\pi\) per tonne of emissions abated below the unpriced baseline \(e_0 Q\): a results-based climate finance facility, a cooperative approach under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, or a bilateral arrangement. With equation 1 and output \(Q\), a feebate at rate \(t\) abates \(Q t / k\) tonnes at resource cost \(Q t^2 / 2k\).

Proposition 6 (crediting). The adopting country’s net cost of a feebate at rate \(t\) is \[ N(t) = \frac{Q\,t\,(t - 2\pi)}{2k}. \tag{4}\] It is negative for \(0 < t < 2\pi\). The country’s best response is \(t = \pi\), which yields a surplus of \(Q\pi^2/2k\), half the buyer’s payment of \(Q\pi^2/k\).

The intuition is that the payment is made at the marginal rate, while the country’s average abatement cost is half its marginal cost under a linear marginal cost curve and below it under any rising curve. A crediting price therefore induces a feebate at the same rate, without any treasury cost, and leaves the country better off (Figure 3).

The buyer’s side. The buyer pays \(\pi\) per tonne. Paying is worthwhile if \(\pi\) is at or below the buyer’s marginal damage from emissions, or below its own marginal abatement cost if the payment counts toward its target. Because the feebate’s marginal incentive equals \(\pi\), the buyer pays exactly the marginal cost of the last tonne, as in an efficient permit market; it overpays the average cost, and the surplus is the price of getting the policy adopted.

Baselines and additionality. The result treats the baseline \(e_0\) as known. In practice the adopting country knows it better than the buyer and has an incentive to overstate it. Three safeguards apply. The baseline can be set from verified historical intensity before the policy was announced; crediting can be on the change in measured intensity rather than its level, so that overstating the baseline has no payoff once the first year is verified; and the policy’s effect can be measured as a carbon-price equivalent, the uniform tax that would produce the same emission change (Stretton 2026d), which separates the policy’s contribution from changes in output and fuel prices. These are the same problems faced by every results-based instrument (Partnership for Market Readiness 2017; World Bank and Frankfurt School of Finance and Management 2017); the feebate makes them easier because it acts directly on the measured variable, intensity.

Who claims the reduction. Proposition 6 assumes the adopting country keeps the reduction toward its own target. If the buyer instead counts it under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, the seller must make a corresponding adjustment and loses the reduction from its own account. It then needs to be paid for the carbon as well as the cost, and the break-even price rises from about half the feebate rate to about one and a half times it (Strand 2020; World Bank 2022). Crediting of policy without transfer of attribution, as in results-based climate finance, is the cheaper route and the one the proposition describes.

Why credit policies rather than projects. Project-based crediting pays for individual installations whose additionality is contested and whose emissions may simply move elsewhere in the sector. A sector-wide feebate moves the whole sector’s intensity, and its rebate leg rewards the same clean installations a project mechanism would, without the counterfactual.

8 From leakage to a race to the top

Let an importing market apply a destination charge \(\tau\) per tonne of embodied carbon, measured at actual intensity. Exporter \(i\) runs a feebate at rate \(t_i\), chooses intensity \(e_i = e_{0i} - t_i/k_i\), and delivers at cost \[ D_i = c_0 + \frac{t_i^2}{2k_i} + \tau\left(e_{0i} - \frac{t_i}{k_i}\right). \tag{5}\]

Proposition 7 (best response). \(D_i\) is minimized at \(t_i = \tau\). Each exporter’s most competitive feebate rate equals the carbon charge in its export markets.

The result is the production-side mirror of Proposition 1: the importer prices the average carbon in what it buys, and each exporter does best by matching the marginal incentive at home. As importers raise \(\tau\), exporters raise \(t_i\). Market share moves toward the producers with the lowest embodied carbon after the response. Under origin-based pricing without border adjustment the opposite happens: production moves toward the lowest carbon price.

The direction of competition has a simple statement. Under origin taxes, a country that raises its carbon price loses market share; under the two tracks, a country that raises its feebate rate toward its export markets’ charges gains it. This is the property that let VAT spread without coordination (Keen and Lockwood 2010), and it is a decentralized form of the club incentive in Nordhaus (2015): no tariff on non-members is needed, because every exporter already faces the charge in its markets.

To quantify the effect, Figure 4 simulates an importing market buying hot-rolled steel from the eight exporters in Table 1, with Armington substitution (\(\sigma = 4\), stylized) and equal shares before any charge. Two cases are compared at each charge \(\tau\): exporters do nothing, so only the composition of imports changes; and exporters set \(t_i = \tau\). At \(\tau = \$100\), the average embodied intensity of imports falls from 3.6 to 2.8 tCO₂/t through composition alone, and to 1.2 tCO₂/t when exporters respond. The most carbon-intensive exporter loses share in both cases, but loses less when it adopts a feebate (2.9 against 2.0 percent of the market): it has the most to gain from adopting.

The condition. Proposition 7 requires that the importer’s charge rise with actual intensity, so that a lower intensity earns a lower charge. A destination charge on verified or rebuttable default intensities satisfies it. The EU’s mechanism satisfies it for intensity but not for policy: it deducts from the importer’s liability only a carbon price “effectively paid” in the country of origin (European Parliament and Council 2023), and a revenue-neutral feebate, by design, has no net price paid. An exporter that adopts a feebate gains through lower intensity, but not through recognition of the policy itself. The legal opening is narrow. Article 9 of the regulation, as replaced in 2025, allows a default carbon price for a country only “where a carbon price was set by the rules applicable in the third country” (European Parliament and Council 2023), so recognition of a feebate needs either a broad reading of that text or an amendment at the scheduled review. The companion paper on CBAM proposes recognizing implicit and non-price instruments through the default carbon-price methodology, measured as carbon-price equivalents (Stretton 2026b, 2026d).

Shuffling. A charge on actual plant intensity has a weakness that Proposition 7 ignores: an exporter with clean and dirty plants can send clean output to the charging market and dirty output elsewhere, cutting its bill without cutting emissions (Bushnell et al. 2014). Standardized values by country and sector avoid this but blunt the incentive for individual plants (Neuhoff et al. 2026). A sector-wide feebate in the exporting country closes the gap from the other side: it lowers intensity across all output, whatever its destination, so there is less to shuffle. Charges set high on country averages also fall hardest on poorer exporters (Mattoo et al. 2009), which is a further reason to recognize the policy rather than only the plant.

Crediting and the race together. An exporter facing both a destination charge \(\tau\) in its markets and a crediting price \(\pi\) chooses a feebate rate between the two that balances its export competitiveness against crediting revenue. Both forces push the rate up from zero, and both reward the most carbon-intensive exporters most for adopting.

9 Implementation

The production track. A feebate needs, for each covered sector, a measure of output, a measure of emissions at the installation, and a benchmark rule. The first two already exist wherever an emissions trading system or a CBAM reporting obligation applies; the EU’s monitoring rules and default values cover cement, iron and steel, aluminium, fertilizers, hydrogen and electricity (European Parliament and Council 2023). The benchmark is the output-weighted average of the previous period, announced in advance. Canada’s output-based pricing system and the free-allocation benchmarks of the EU system are working precedents for the benchmark side (Stretton 2026c).

The consumption track, goods. The carbon component of VAT is a charge per unit of embodied carbon added to the existing VAT on each good, with the value component reduced so that the total burden changes little at the start (Stretton 2026a). Domestic goods carry a sector-average embodied intensity through the VAT chain; imports carry rebuttable default intensities set generously at the outset, so that the charge does not provoke a trade dispute, with importers free to prove a lower value; exports are zero-rated, as in VAT. Keen, Parry and Roaf recommend the same sequence of domestic benchmarks first and country-specific values later (Keen et al. 2022).

The consumption track, energy. Fuel sold for domestic heating and transport is burned after the last sale, so its carbon is embodied in no good and the VAT component cannot reach it; and a few large firms dominate its supply: fuel importers, refiners, gas suppliers. For these the consumption track is a legal obligation, announced in advance and rising on a published path, to account for the carbon in what they sell. An obligation announced years ahead gives the firms that plan the capital stock the forward price that a tax set annually cannot credibly give (Kydland and Prescott 1977; Helm 2003). Electricity is different: it is sold on an invoice, so where a VAT carbon component exists it carries the generation carbon to the final user, net of the production-track price already paid (Stretton 2026a). Where it does not, as in most developing countries at the start, the obligation can be extended to electricity retailers on the same net basis.

Measurement. Each track needs its effect expressed on a common scale for two purposes: recognition at foreign borders, and crediting. The carbon-price-equivalent metric of Stretton (2026d) expresses any instrument, price-based or not, as the uniform carbon tax that would produce the same emission change. A country that regulates rather than taxes can then claim the same recognition as one that prices. The IMF’s framework for comparing mitigation policies across countries takes the same approach for price and non-price instruments (Black et al. 2022). Equal carbon-price equivalents mean equal emission effects, not equal costs to firms: a standard and a tax with the same equivalent impose different private costs, and a border rule built on the metric should say which it is matching.

Trade law. The consumption charge is an internal tax applied equally to domestic and imported goods and is adjustable at the border under GATT Articles II:2(a) and III:2; the open question is whether carbon intensity, a process characteristic, can differentiate otherwise like products (Mehling et al. 2019; Ismer and Neuhoff 2007). The feebate is a sector-wide charge-and-rebate scheme, not contingent on export performance; its rebate leg needs care under the Agreement on Subsidies and Countervailing Measures, which a sector-wide, formula-based scheme is designed to satisfy. A full legal analysis is outside the scope of this paper.

10 Objections and limits

Distribution. A carbon component of VAT is regressive if carbon-intensive goods form a larger share of poorer households’ spending. Because the reform cuts the value component as the carbon component rises, the net effect depends on the difference in carbon intensity across budgets rather than on the level of carbon prices; it should be measured with household expenditure data before rates are set.

Double charging in mixed regimes. A good exported from a country with an origin carbon tax to one with a destination charge would pay twice unless the exporter zero-rates its exports, as the destination principle requires, or the importer deducts the origin price. In a transition, the importer’s deduction for carbon prices paid, as under CBAM, is the stopgap. The feebate does not create this problem: it has no net payment on average and so nothing to deduct, which is exactly why recognition must rest on the price signal rather than the payment (Section 8).

Accounting under the Paris Agreement. National targets are set on territorial emissions. The production track reduces territorial emissions directly; the consumption track reduces them at home and abroad. A country adopting both gets credit for the first under its target and contributes to others’ targets through the second.

Capacity. Countries without a functioning VAT cannot run the goods part of the consumption track. They can run the production track, which needs only sector intensity data, and that is where their emissions are.

General equilibrium. The model is partial equilibrium. Factor-market interactions, the use of revenue and exchange-rate effects all matter for welfare. The results on intensity, residual cost, crediting and best response do not depend on them; the welfare ranking against a uniform carbon tax does.

11 Conclusion

A carbon price levied on production does two jobs with one rate, and in an open economy the second job undermines the first. Pricing production intensity with a revenue-neutral feebate and consumption with a destination-based charge gives each job its own instrument. Together they reproduce the Pigouvian allocation for domestic consumption without leakage; the production track costs a third or less of a tax in producer prices; crediting at a price above half the feebate rate makes adoption a gain; and destination charges make each exporter’s most competitive feebate rate equal to the charge in its markets. The open work is empirical calibration of abatement costs by sector, the legal text for the consumption charge, and the border rules that recognize instruments that price carbon without a price paid.

12 Appendix A: Literature review

This appendix reviews the literature behind each proposition, organized by theme. The working notes behind it, with a summary of each paper and how it was read (full text, abstract or metadata), are in 5.Notes/LiteratureAppendix-draft.md.

12.1 A.1 Where the architecture sits

The two-track architecture joins four bodies of work that have mostly developed apart: the theory of unilateral policy under leakage, border carbon adjustment, intensity-based instruments, and destination-based taxation.

The theory of the split is old. Markusen (1975) showed that with an international externality the best unilateral policy taxes both production and consumption. Hoel (1996) showed that without tariffs a carbon tax should be lower in trade-exposed sectors. Weisbach et al. (2023) restate the result in modern form and add an extraction leg. Most directly, Stephen P. Holland (2012) proves that an intensity standard combined with a consumption tax can reach the first best under leakage, while an emissions tax combined with a consumption tax sometimes cannot. Proposition 1 is therefore an implementable statement of a known allocation result, not a new theorem. Its revenue corollary, that the tracks differ by \(t\) times carbon in net exports, is the carbon analogue of the neutrality of origin and destination bases for a uniform tax (Lockwood and Whalley 2010; Lockwood et al. 1994).

The design has close European precedents. Grubb et al. (2022) list the separation of incentives at the point of production from a charge on the use of carbon-intensive materials as one of three trade-compatible options. Pollitt et al. (2020) simulate a consumption charge on basic materials equivalent to about €80/tCO₂: it cuts EU emissions by roughly 10 percent with no leakage. Ismer et al. (2016) give the legal design of such a charge as an excise at default intensity, applied equally to imports. Neuhoff et al. (2026) propose benchmark-based free allocation plus a standardized liability per tonne of material with export relief. Each is a production-plus-consumption architecture.

What this paper adds is narrower: (i) a revenue-neutral feebate with an updated benchmark in place of free allocation, so the production track needs no emissions trading system and no auction revenue and can be adopted by a developing country alone; (ii) a consumption track that runs through VAT across all goods rather than an excise on a few materials; (iii) the closed-form residual cost \(\tfrac12 t\Delta e\) and its calibration to EU default intensities for steel; (iv) the exporter best response under intensity-based destination charges; and (v) the extension of Strand’s crediting threshold to feebates, with the best response \(t = \pi\).

12.2 A.2 Leakage and competitiveness

Model-based estimates of leakage from unilateral carbon pricing range from 5 to 25 percent, with a central value of about 14 percent (Branger and Quirion 2014). Ex-post studies of the EU system find little or none at prices to date (Naegele and Zaklan 2019; Dechezleprêtre et al. 2022; Colmer et al. 2025), partly because free allocation shields industry and partly because prices were low; the evidence on relocation of investment is similar (Dechezleprêtre and Sato 2017). Pass-through of cost shocks is incomplete in EU trade-exposed sectors and about 70 percent in US manufacturing (Ganapati et al. 2020). The case for the architecture is therefore prospective: it concerns the rates of $80–100 that the range of the High-Level Commission implies (High-Level Commission on Carbon Prices 2017), not leakage already observed. A second leakage channel, through world fossil-fuel prices, survives any charge on goods (Branger and Quirion 2014; Weisbach et al. 2023); only supply-side measures or wider participation address it (Jakob et al. 2014).

12.3 A.3 Border carbon adjustment

Keen et al. (2022) is the reference design paper: border adjustments are the most effective domestic response to leakage, design is critical, coverage should start with energy-intensive trade-exposed sectors, and charges should be benchmarked first on domestic intensities. Mehling et al. (2019) analyze border adjustments under GATT Articles I, II:2(a), III and XX and the subsidies agreement, and recommend default values with rebuttal and credit for foreign policies, which supports the recognition of non-price instruments argued here and in Stretton (2026b). Cosbey et al. (2019) give design guidance in the same direction. On distribution, Mattoo et al. (2009) find that charges on the carbon content of imports, if exporters do not respond, cut manufacturing exports from low- and middle-income countries by about 8 percent and China’s by about a fifth. The EU’s mechanism (European Parliament and Council 2023) as amended, with default values that carry deliberate mark-ups (European Commission 2025), deducts only carbon prices effectively paid, a choice examined in the companion paper (Stretton 2026b).

12.4 A.4 Intensity-based instruments and feebates

Carolyn Fischer (2001) shows that tradable performance standards, taxes with output-based rebates and output-based permit allocation are all equivalent to an emissions tax plus an output subsidy: for a given target they lean too much on intensity and too little on output. That is Proposition 4. Stephen P. Holland et al. (2009) show that intensity standards can even raise emissions where the output subsidy dominates. C. Fischer and Fox (2007) and Carolyn Fischer and Fox (2012) compare output-based rebates with border adjustment: full adjustment is the most effective against leakage, but where it is limited a domestic rebate can do more. The evidence from feebates in use is mixed in the expected direction. The Swedish NOx charge, refunded on output, cut emission intensity substantially (Sterner and Höglund Isaksson 2006). The French bonus-malus on cars shifted purchases toward low-emission models but raised total emissions in the short run through higher sales (D’Haultfœuille et al. 2014). The IMF finds feebate packages achieve roughly 50–70 percent of the cuts of a carbon tax at the same rate (International Monetary Fund 2019).

12.5 A.5 Destination and origin

For a uniform, broad-based tax, a switch between origin and destination bases changes price levels, not relative prices, and so has no real trade effects (Lockwood and Whalley 2010; Lockwood et al. 1994). Proposition 7 therefore rests on the non-uniformity of carbon charges across exporters’ intensities, not on the destination basis as such. VAT shows that a destination-based tax can spread without coordination (Keen and Lockwood 2010); proposals for destination-based corporate taxation rest on the same logic (Auerbach et al. 2017; Devereux et al. 2021). Consumption-based accounts show that the footprints of high-income countries exceed their territorial emissions (Peters and Hertwich 2008; Peters et al. 2011; Davis and Caldeira 2010).

12.6 A.6 Clubs and the race to the top

Nordhaus (2015) shows that a club with a small uniform tariff on non-members can sustain a large coalition. The incentive in Proposition 7 differs: it comes from a charge that rises with each exporter’s intensity, not from a flat penalty. Böhringer et al. (2016) find the threat of carbon tariffs credible in a numerical game, and Helm et al. (2012) argue that border adjustments give exporters an incentive to price carbon themselves so as to keep the revenue.

12.7 A.7 Crediting and results-based finance

Strand (2020) derives, for a donor-supported carbon tax, a break-even payment of half the tax rate when the host keeps the reduction toward its own target, the same threshold as Proposition 6, rising to about one and a half times the rate when the credit is transferred with a corresponding adjustment under Article 6 (World Bank 2022). The case for crediting policy rather than projects rests on the poor record of project offsets: fewer than 16 percent of credits examined by Probst et al. (2024) represent real reductions, and Calel et al. (2025) find at least half of Indian wind credits non-additional. Baselines remain the hard part (Partnership for Market Readiness 2017; World Bank and Frankfurt School of Finance and Management 2017).

12.8 A.8 Credibility and forward obligations

A government that re-optimizes each period cannot commit, so a carbon price set annually will not be believed by investors in long-lived capital (Kydland and Prescott 1977). Once firms have sunk low-carbon investment, governments are tempted to lower the price, and firms anticipate this (Helm 2003; Brunner et al. 2012). A forward-announced legal obligation on the few large suppliers of fuel and electricity is a commitment device of the kind this literature recommends.

12.9 A.9 Literature that challenges a proposition

Proposition Challenge Source Response in the paper
1 (no leakage) Leakage through world fuel prices survives any charge on goods Branger and Quirion (2014); Weisbach et al. (2023) Stated as the fourth qualification to Proposition 1
1 (novelty) Intensity standard plus consumption tax already shown first best Stephen P. Holland (2012) Proposition 1 presented as an implementable statement of a known result
4–5 (output margin) Intensity instruments can raise output and emissions Stephen P. Holland et al. (2009); D’Haultfœuille et al. (2014) Sign condition (Proposition 5); consumption track supplies the output margin
6 (crediting) Threshold rises to about \(1.5t\) with a corresponding adjustment Strand (2020); World Bank (2022) Proposition 6 restricted to crediting without transfer of attribution
7 (race to the top) Charges on actual intensity invite shuffling; standardized values preferred Neuhoff et al. (2026); Bushnell et al. (2014) A sector-wide feebate lowers intensity on all output, leaving less to shuffle
7 (development cost) Charges on the carbon content of imports cut developing-country exports if exporters do not respond Mattoo et al. (2009) The best response is to adopt the feebate, and recognition should rest on the price signal

13 Appendix B: Proofs

Setup. Unit cost \(c(e) = c_0 + \tfrac{k}{2}(e_0 - e)^2\); competitive pricing, \(p = c(e) + {}\)policy payment per unit; baseline \(p_0 = c_0\).

Proposition 2. Under the origin tax the firm minimizes \(c(e) + te\); under the feebate, \(c(e) + t(e - \bar e)\) with \(\bar e\) taken as given. In both cases the first-order condition is \(k(e_0 - e) = t\), so \(e^* = e_0 - t/k\) and \(\Delta e = t/k\); the second-order condition holds since \(c''(e) = k > 0\).

Proposition 3. Under the feebate with \(\bar e = e^*\), net payments are zero and \(p_F = c(e^*) = c_0 + t^2/2k\); since \(\Delta e = t/k\), \(t^2/2k = \tfrac12 t \Delta e\). Under the tax, \(p_T = c(e^*) + t e^* = c_0 + t e_0 - t^2/2k\). The ratio is \((t^2/2k)/(te_0 - t^2/2k) = \Delta e/(2e_0 - \Delta e)\). Output changes follow from \(\Delta Q/Q \approx -\eta\, \Delta p / p_0\).

Proposition 1. (i) follows from Proposition 2. (ii) Under the two tracks a home-produced unit consumed at home costs \(c(e^*) + t(e^* - \bar e) + \tau e^*\); with \(\bar e = e^*\) and \(\tau = t\) this is \(c(e^*) + t e^*\), the Pigouvian price. An imported unit with embodied intensity \(m\) costs its delivered price plus \(\tau m\). (iii) An exported unit costs \(c(e^*) + t(e^* - \bar e) = c(e^*)\). Revenue: the feebate raises zero in total; the destination charge raises \(\tau\) times embodied carbon in home consumption. The origin tax raises \(t\) times emissions from home production. With \(\tau = t\), the difference is \(t\) times (carbon in home production minus carbon in home consumption), which is \(t\) times carbon embodied in net exports.

Proposition 4. To first order, tonnes abated under the tax are \(Q\,\Delta e + e_0\,|\Delta Q| = Q t_T/k + e_0 Q \eta t_T e_0 / p_0\); under the feebate alone, \(Q t_F / k\) (the output change is second order). Equating gives \(t_F = t_T (1 + \eta k e_0^2 / p_0)\).

Proposition 5. With a competitive fringe, the price equals the marginal producer’s unit cost, \(c_m(e_m^*) + t(e_m^* - \bar e) = c_{0m} + \tfrac12 t \Delta e_m + t(e_m^* - \bar e)\). Output falls relative to no policy if and only if this exceeds \(c_{0m}\).

Proposition 6. \(N(t) = Q t^2/2k - \pi Q t/k = Q t (t - 2\pi)/2k\). \(N(t) < 0\) for \(0 < t < 2\pi\); \(N'(t) = Q(t - \pi)/k = 0\) at \(t = \pi\), where \(N = -Q\pi^2/2k\). The buyer pays \(\pi \cdot Q\pi/k = Q\pi^2/k\).

Proposition 7. \(\partial D_i / \partial t_i = (t_i - \tau)/k_i = 0\) at \(t_i = \tau\), and \(\partial^2 D_i / \partial t_i^2 = 1/k_i > 0\).

All results were checked symbolically.

14 Appendix C: Calibration and simulation

Data. EU default values for embodied emissions, direct emissions in tCO₂ per tonne, as adopted under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621; extracted for cement (CN 2523 29), semi-finished steel (7207 11 11), hot-rolled flat steel (7208) and unwrought aluminium (7601) for 120 countries and the residual “other countries” category in 2.Source/CBAM-default-values-steel-aluminium-cement.csv. The default values used in the EU’s regime from 2026 add a mark-up of 10 percent in 2026, 20 percent in 2027 and 30 percent from 2028 for steel; the calibration uses the values before mark-up, which are the better estimate of actual intensity.

Stylized parameters. Base price $600/t for all exporters [VERIFY against hot-rolled coil export prices]; abatement slope \(k_i = 50/(0.3\,e_{0i})\), so that $50/tCO₂ cuts intensity by 30 percent; an abatement floor at 30 percent of baseline intensity; Armington elasticity \(\sigma = 4\) among exporters [VERIFY against estimates for steel]; equal preference weights.

Code. 2.Source/simulate_steel.py writes Table 1, Figure 2 and Figure 4; 2.Source/make_fig1_incidence.py writes Figure 1.

15 Appendix D: Political feasibility

Let industry accept a policy if the rise in its average cost is at most \(\bar c_I\), and voters accept it if the rise in household prices net of rebates is at most \(\bar c_V\). Under an origin tax at rate \(t\), industry’s average cost rises by \(t e_0 - t^2/2k \approx t e_0\), and households’ prices by \(\alpha t\), where \(\alpha\) is the carbon embodied per dollar of household spending. The feasible rate is \(t^{\max}_{\text{tax}} = \min(\bar c_I / e_0,\ \bar c_V / \alpha)\). Under the two tracks, industry’s average cost rises by \(t^2/2k\), so the industry constraint allows \(t \le \sqrt{2k\,\bar c_I}\), which exceeds \(\bar c_I/e_0\) whenever \(\bar c_I < 2 k e_0^2\), that is, whenever the industry constraint binds at any rate cutting intensity by less than its full baseline. The household constraint applies to the consumption rate \(\tau\) net of the VAT cut. The production rate is no longer limited by what households will accept, and the consumption rate is no longer limited by what industry will accept. That separation is the political case for the architecture.
